vignette: He carries the quiet tension of a coiled spring when he first steps into the room. He settles into the chair, his eyes mapping the exits, and slowly pieces together the story he has been carrying since the kitchen door clicked shut that afternoon. The first strike arrives without warning, a sudden rupture in everything he thought they shared. He learns quickly how to curl inward, how to make himself small, how to count the hairline fractures in the ceiling plaster until the violence passes. When it stops, silence settles heavy and thick. He watches his own hands tremble against his knees and wonders how the same arms that once braided his hair could now turn into weights. In the weeks that follow, he moves through his apartment like a ghost, sweeping glass into dustpans, washing sheets until the fabric grows thin. He tells no one. He carries the quiet expectations of an African upbringing, where male suffering is folded into duty and never spoken aloud. He deletes the messages, erases the photos, and begins to rebuild his reality on paper. His work as a curriculum designer demands structure, a clear sequence of objectives, and a predictable path from point A to point B. For months, he tries to pour that same order into his days. He drafts lesson frameworks until his eyes blur, mapping out competencies and assessment rubrics as if precision could anchor him. He catches himself rewriting the same learning outcomes twelve times, chasing a clarity he cannot find in his own body. His cursor blinks like a metronome, counting down to mistakes that never come. But the architecture of his nervous system refuses to cooperate. He finds himself pausing mid-sentence during team calls, suddenly aware of the hum of his laptop fan, the rhythm of his own breathing, the weight of his shoes against the floor. He starts avoiding shared workspaces, preferring the isolation of his home office. When colleagues mention weekend plans or pair up for coffee, he makes quiet excuses. The world feels too loud, too unpredictable. He sleeps on the living room floor for three weeks because the mattress feels like a trap, and he keeps a heavy flashlight in the hallway, telling himself it is for power outages, though the grid has not failed in months. Small things become landmines. The sharp click of a car door down the street sends his shoulders up to his ears. He scans restaurant booths, always choosing the corner seat with his back to the wall, eyes tracking every entrance, memorizing exits. He has started wearing noise-canceling headphones in public, not for focus, but to dampen the sudden spikes of sound that mimic the cadence of raised voices. His phone, once a window to his friends, now rests face-down, vibrating with phantom alarms. He cancels dates after the first coffee, citing sudden work deadlines, when what he really feels is a cold dread pooling in his stomach. He replays the kitchen that afternoon on a loop, bargaining in silence with versions of himself that could have spoken sooner, could have left earlier. He tells himself he is strong because he still shows up, because he still drafts modules that help other people learn, but inside, he feels fractured, like a document saved in an old format, struggling to open. At thirty, he lives alone in a quiet building with thick walls and a reliable lock. He waters his plants, walks the same route to the grocery store, and opens his design software each morning to arrange fonts and pacing guides. He does not believe he will ever date again. He does not believe he will ever feel entirely safe in his own skin. Some nights, the old tension wakes him at 3 a.m., and he sits by the window until the sky lightens, listening to the city breathe around him. He does not call it recovery. He calls it showing up. He arranges his files, checks his schedule, and waits for the next module to take shape, knowing that some frameworks can be built by hand, while others must simply be survived.
